topics.title: Simple(r) Problems Marathon
topics.text:
Just wanted to start a marathon of relatively simple problems (like AMC #5-12 difficulty). Thought it would be fun to take a break from more complex math and that it would be helpful for beginners who are looking to do well on AMC. Hopefully this is interesting and different from the many marathons that already exist on AoPS. Don't post problems that are super difficult, but also don't post problems that are ridiculously easy. Problems can be pretty much any topic.



EDIT:

Rules -

1. Please post a solution to the previous problem and a new problem each time, hide your problem and solution using this format: [code]P1PROBLEM
[/code]

2. Post relatively simple problems, nothing harder than AMC 10 #15 difficulty

3. Have fun!

topics.title: How to Change My Approach to the 10B
topics.text:
First of all, sorry I had to post this here, since the Contests forum got locked. Now, I failed the AMC10A pretty badly, yielding a score around 48 pts below my goal and racking up 8 sillies among the first 16 problems. However, I solved 22 problems, and obviously did not get anything near 132 or even 120. The first 10 problems had taken slightly longer than expected, and I fakesolved a few of them even (and this totally backfired). It took me forever to solve #14, and decided I would skip it the first time I looked at it. I couldn't solve 17 and 20. However, I still guessed an answer for them without even eliminating any choices, knowing that I was doing horribly- and I guessed wrong. However, I got some of the harder problems right, including #18. This made me think that the sillies were mainly due to pressure.



Now my goal for the 10B is just to make AIME. How should my approach change from the way I took the 10A? How should I deal with time pressure? Should I guess less often, or be even more reckless? What do people think about fake-solving when the problems are really easy anyway? I can definitely solve 23 problems during practice tests, but the pressure of the real test crushes me. Any tips are appreciated.



Finally, I know many threads similar to this have been made, but none of the tips were very applicable to me. Thanks.

topics.title: Math Contest Problem 4
topics.text:
This question is about mathematically correct conclusions, not whether parts of the following statements are true on their own or not.



Which of the following conclusions was NOT performed correctly:

a) 21 is a factor of 84 and 3 is a factor of 21. Therefore, 3 must be a factor of 84.

b) 19 is a prime number. Because 5 is not equal to 1 and not equal to 19, 5 can not be a factor of 19.

c) Although we know that 5 x 8 = 40 and 40 is divisible by 4, this alone is not enough to conclude that 8 is divisible by 4.

d) Because 4 and 9 have no common factors other than 1, the smallest common multiple of 4 and 9 must be 4 x 9 = 36.

e) We know that 2 is not a factor of 5 and 2 is not a factor of 7. Therefore 2 can not be a factor of 5 x 7 = 35.

topics.title: The "How many times do they pass each other" Question
topics.text:
Hello there! I seem to be stuck (on nearly every single math contest) on the "how many times do two people pass each other question." What are some approaches?

___________________________________________________________________________________________________

Example

A and B run in opposite directions on a circular track. A finishes the track in 10 seconds while B finishes in 20; they continue running for 10 minutes: how many times do they pass each other?

IMAGE

__________________________________________________________________________________________________

What are some approaches to this?

Thanks!

-Chgon

_________________________________________________________________________________________________



Responses:

Thanks for the responses! This is for easy access so people don't repost!

fishy15's response[quote=fishy15]For these problems where everything is vague, I like to assign values to each of the things. I would say in the example that that the track is 100 meters long. A runs 10 m/s and B runs 5 m/s. Then we make a circle and assign a starting point. Find out where they first meet and after how much time. That is the time between meetings, so divide that by 10 minutes and you should get the answer.[/quote]


_________________________________________________________________________________________________

"What have you done to approach this," I am just stuck on how to tackle the problem. Or the logic part of the problem.

topics.title: Funny/Weird Intro to Number Theory Problem
topics.text:
Introduction to Number Theory Problem 9.25:



The evil villain Harris Pilton wrote three secret two-digit numbers, $x$, $y$, and $z$ on a napkin. Berris Fueler must name three numbers $A$, $B$, and $C$, after which Harris will announce the value of $Ax+By+Cz$. If Berris can then name Harris' three secret numbers, Harris will let Berris go. Save Berris! Come up with a way to choose $A$, $B$, and $C$ such that Berris is sure to escape Harris' evil clutches.



The answer is $A=10,000, B=100, $ and $C=1$, but the funny/weird thing is that this is an obvious reference to Paris Hilton(Harris Pilton, first letters are switched) and Berris Fueler(Ferris Bueller, first letters are also switched). Why is it like that?

topics.title: Genetic Disorder Problem (is math problem, not bio)
topics.text:
Trasha discovered new genetic material TNA (The New Alien), impacts chance of getting ramin, a disease. Trasha has three possible nucleobases, Alien, Graxa, Calyposo. Each Alien increases chance that owner has ramio by 3%, Graxa decreases chance by 2%, and Calyposo does not affect. Suppose that Trasha can choose the nucleobases on his XNA of length 420 and that his goal is to have exactly 1% chance of getting ramin. What is the probability he succeeds if he is smart scientist and choose optimally?



% refer to percentage points. Negative probability means he has chance of curing it.

topics.title: Problem Wording?
topics.text:
On my car, a particular brand of tire lasts 1000 miles on a front wheel or 2000 miles on a rear wheel. By switching the front and rear tires, what is the greatest distance, in miles I can get from a set of four of these tires?



Apparently the answer is just the average of the wear on the $4$ wheels, which is $4000/3$.  But wouldn't the answer just be $1000$ because once you used up the front tires, you can't run any furthur?  Am I missing something?
